      <title>Paper trail of protests: José Mourinho plays the hits in Madrid derby defeat | Sid Lowe</title>
      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/football/2026/sep/21/real-madrid-atletico-madrid-jose-mourinho-diego-simeone-madrid-derby-la-liga</link>
      <description><p>Facing Diego Simeone 13 years on, José Mourinho brought a print-out and paranoia. Some things don’t change. Some people don’t, either</p><p>There were many questions to emerge from the Madrid derby, which <a href="http://www.theguardian.com/football/2026/sep/20/atletico-madrid-real-madrid-la-liga-match-report">Atlético won 2-1 </a>in front of 70,514 very, very noisy people at the Metropolitano on Sunday afternoon, even if not the one José Mourinho was asking. Like: what year is this? Or: what was Dean Huijsen thinking? Why always Arda? And whatever happened to Vinícius Júnior? How come Koke is <em>still</em> the best? And how long before Giuliano Simeone <em>actually</em> bursts, his <em>atlético</em> insides exploding across the pitch? Above all though, you were left wondering: where did Real Madrid’s manager get a printer from? And how did he get the bloody thing to work?</p><p>You could still hear the singing outside when Mourinho turned up in the press room, laid down his glasses and sat. In his hand was a piece of paper. Thirteen years after his last derby, on the Santiago Bernabéu night when <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/football/2013/may/18/atletico-madrid-real-copa-del-rey">Madrid lost the Copa del Rey final</a> and a <em>13-year</em> unbeaten run against their neighbours, Diego Simeone had defeated him again. The stage was new – <a href="http://www.theguardian.com/football/blog/2017/sep/18/a-stadium-called-wanda-opening-night-at-atletico-madrids-new-home">this stadium didn’t exist then</a> – but his adversary was somehow still the same man, still dressed in black, and the scene was a bit like old times, a classic. Mourinho unfolded the paper and held it up. “We can save ourselves the bother of the press conference,” he said, “because the story is right here.”</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/football/2026/sep/21/real-madrid-atletico-madrid-jose-mourinho-diego-simeone-madrid-derby-la-liga">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <title>Jonathan David earns Atlético precious win over 10-man Real Madrid in fractious derby</title>
      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/football/2026/sep/20/atletico-madrid-real-madrid-la-liga-match-report</link>
      <description><p>On the eve of the derby, Diego Simeone described this as a special week in Madrid, a “tremendous energy about the city”, and it closed the way he wanted. He had enjoyed the Formula One, he said, and he had enjoyed seeing Shakira in concert, but he enjoyed this even more. At least he did by the time the last of many, many blows on the referee’s whistle brought it to an end, sprinting up the tunnel punching the air. Having been 2-0 up against 10 men through goals from Álex Grimaldo and Jonathan David, seemingly in control, a late header from Antonio Rüdiger awoke old ghosts and brought tension, but they did it.</p><p>“A lot has happened in the city but this was the only thing that mattered in his mind and mine,” Atletico keeper Jan Oblak said afterwards. José Mourinho’s first derby back at Real Madrid ended in defeat and recriminations: he turned up in the press conference with a picture of two moments in which he claimed that Lee Kang-in and Cristian Romero should have been sent off and insisted the story was there. And yet there are other questions: over the way Dean Huijsen gave away the penalty and got the red card that tilted the game against them, and how his team played, how little they did.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/football/2026/sep/20/atletico-madrid-real-madrid-la-liga-match-report">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <title>Case not proven: Trent Alexander-Arnold’s England recall is based on patchy evidence</title>
      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/football/2026/sep/18/trent-alexander-arnold-england-recall-patchy-evidence</link>
      <description><p>Thomas Tuchel promises to play the full-back in his natural right-sided position but we have not seen enough of him this term to gauge his form</p><p>Thomas Tuchel said Trent Alexander Arnold had enjoyed a good start to the season, which came as news to those in England who have not been watching him at Real Madrid. It also, in truth, came as news to those in Spain who have. If the England manager did not see enough in Alexander-Arnold to include him in the World Cup in the summer he has not really had the chance to see enough to change that decision as autumn begins. Two unremarkable league starts provide insufficient evidence with which to make a case for the full-back’s recall, or indeed his exclusion, but he is in the squad.</p><p>Alexander-Arnold’s most high-profile match this season has been <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/football/2026/sep/08/real-madrid-inter-champions-league-match-report">against Inter at the Santiago Bernabéu</a>. That night, he started from the middle of midfield.       <title>Carlos Espí gives Real Madrid hope in the face of Barcelona’s La Liga storm | Sid Lowe</title>
      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/football/2026/sep/17/carlos-espi-real-madrid-barcelona-mourinho-la-liga</link>
      <description><p>With Barcelona racking up seven-goal thrillers, Real Madrid could not afford a collapse. Enter the forward quietly turning into José Mourinho’s ultimate secret weapon</p><p>José Mourinho called and Carlos Espí came to his side. It was late, it was noisy and it was almost over – the match and maybe even something more – when Real Madrid’s coach took the forward who is also his flatmate to one side on Tuesday night. Standing close, Mourinho had a message to deliver; he also had a piece of paper. Small, folded, half-hidden in his hand, it was not big enough for much more than a single word, shown almost surreptitiously, the request written on it, like what he had whispered in Espí’s ear, <a href="https://x.com/sidlowe/status/2100074458664825169">left to your imagination</a>. <em>Put ball in goal</em>, perhaps. Or: <em>Help</em>. So he did.</p><p>Madrid needed him to, which they should not have. Two goals up inside half an hour at Elche on Tuesday night, they could have added a third or a fourth, maybe even a fifth, before half-time. But, thinking it was as done as it really should have been, their minds perhaps on Sunday’s derby at Atlético too, they had stopped again, drifting. Vinícius Júnior had gone, Arda Guler had gone, Aurélien Tchouaméni might as well have done, barely able to move any more, and now, somehow, the game was going. Goals from Abiel Osorio in the 71st minute and Fer Niño in the 83rd had made it 2-2.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/football/2026/sep/17/carlos-espi-real-madrid-barcelona-mourinho-la-liga">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <description><p><a href="https://www.theguardian.com/info/2022/nov/14/football-daily-email-sign-up"><strong>Sign up now! Sign up now! Sign up now? Sign up now!</strong></a></p><p>Anxious to sample some traditional Spanish culture while taking in a La Liga match years ago, Football Daily and some friends decamped to Gran Alicant. As we prepared to leave a quaint bodega (the Dick Turpin), where we’d been sampling the local hooch (Guinness), to travel to the nearby stadium, an elderly local resident with an unmistakable mackem accent informed us that the Elche home game to which we were heading was not being played until the following evening. It had fallen victim to Spanish TV’s infuriating habit of rescheduling random top-flight matches with little or no notice or consideration for Johnny-come-latelys who might have travelled from afar to watch them. We never did get to see Elche play in the flesh but did get to watch the current La Liga basement-dwellers give José Mourinho an almighty fright on TV on Tuesday night, as they went <em>this</em> close to snatching a point from Real Madrid.</p><p>I almost wish I was a West Ham fan. As an eternally suffering Spurs supporter, I find myself looking enviously towards the London Stadium these days. The Hammers are top of the table, banging in goal after goal (already 20 more than Spurs’ tally in the league). They score even when they lose and seem to have bought a proper No 9. My Spurs, meanwhile, continue the tradition of the last two years in style, sitting comfortably in 17th with 1,047 wingers on contract, and getting knocked out of one of the competitions they could ‘conceivably’ have won, the only competition they seem to be able to score goals in as well. In hindsight, West Ham made the right choice to go down. Hammers fans, you are welcome!” – Yannick Woudstra (and no others).</p><p>Hugh Fordham’s idea [<a href="https://www.theguardian.com/football/2026/sep/15/football-daily-email-leeds-not-disunited">Tuesday’s Football Daily letters</a>] has some merit. But it reminded me of a pithy comment by Bill Nicholson. ‘Do you think he was interfering with play?’, he was asked. Nicholson responded: “If he’s not interfering with play, what’s he doing on the pitch?!’” – Harry McDonald.</p><p>In support of Hugh Fordham’s suggestion, I remember discussing the idea of interfering with play while on a training course for referees back in the 1960s. We were told that unless someone was ‘lying injured near the corner flag’ any player should be treated as being involved in play. Not a lot of room for subjectivity in those days. And obviously no thought of stopping play for the hypothetical injured player!” – Trevor Field.</p><p><em><strong>This is an extract from our daily football email … Football Daily. To get the full version,<a href="https://preview.gutools.co.uk/info/2016/jan/05/the-fiver-email-sign-up"> </a><a href="https://www.theguardian.com/info/2022/nov/14/football-daily-email-sign-up">just visit this page and follow the instructions</a>.</strong></em> </p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/football/2026/sep/16/real-madrid-elche-t-shirts-football-daily-newsletter">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <description><p>Director Joe Pearlman says he expected Real Madrid manager to ‘try to manipulate us’ in making of Netflix series</p><p>Even in the hyperreal world of football, there are few characters more compelling, more polarising, or more everything than José Mourinho, the best and worst of public him on full display in <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/tv-and-radio/2026/aug/11/mourinho-review-if-he-didnt-want-to-open-up-maybe-he-shouldnt-have-starred-in-a-docuseries">a new three-part Netflix series</a>. “It reminded me how good he was,” says Joe Pearlman, who directed Mourinho, and the actual Mourinho is, believe it or not, keen to communicate the same. As he puts it in the show: “I look, you look, I see more than you.”</p><p>Making documentaries, though, is often about taking people to the places they’re most skilled at avoiding. “I knew the interviews were going to be very intense,” says Pearlman, “and he was going to try and control the narrative and manipulate us. Everything bad is everyone else’s fault and everything he’s done is validated by winning. Because that’s all that’s important.”</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/football/2026/aug/18/jose-mourinho-netflix-series-director-interview-joe-pearlman">Continue reading...</a></description>
